intrigue

in-TREEG -- stress on the second syllable when used as a verb (unlike the noun 'IN-treeg,' meaning secret scheming). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To intrigue is to arouse the curiosity or interest of someone.

The unsolved case continued to intrigue amateur detectives decades after it was closed.

Example

A locked room with no visible entrance sits untouched in an old mansion for a hundred years, and its mystery intrigues every visitor who hears about it -- everyone wants to know what's inside.

That pull of curiosity, wanting to know more, is exactly what it means to be intrigued. Unlike 'bore,' which drives attention away, intrigue draws it in.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fascinate: To fascinate is to grip someone's attention with a thing's own strange or remarkable qualities -- people stare, study it, and puzzle over how it works. To intrigue is quieter: it stirs the wish to find out more. A thing can fascinate even while it unsettles you.

pique: To pique someone's curiosity is to give it a quick, sharp poke -- a single odd detail is enough, and the feeling may pass in a minute. To intrigue is to keep that curiosity pulling, so the person stays caught, turning the puzzle over and wanting more.

absorb: To absorb someone is to soak up their attention in a task -- a good project can absorb a whole afternoon. To intrigue is narrower: it hooks curiosity specifically, the itch to find out more, whether or not the person can do anything about it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bore: to make someone feel weary through dullness

repel: to cause a feeling of strong dislike or disgust

Where it sits · how strongly it pulls attention — interest → intrigue → captivate

interest vs. intrigue: Interest is milder than intrigue -- interest can describe a passing curiosity, while intrigue implies a stronger pull that makes someone want to investigate further.

captivate vs. intrigue: Captivate can feel even stronger than intrigue: intrigue draws someone's curiosity in, while captivate holds their attention so completely they can hardly look away.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: into (Latin)

Root — trigue

Root — trigue: to entangle (from Latin tricae, 'perplexities, tricky snares,' via intricare, 'to entangle')

Put it together

Put it together: In- ('into') + trigue ('to entangle' — from Latin tricae, 'perplexities, tricky snares,' via intricare): to intrigue someone, at its root, is to entangle their attention in something puzzling — the same Latin root that gives us intricate.

Use the root in a new word: intricate

Use the root in a new word: intricate: The watchmaker admired the intricate gears fitted precisely inside the tiny case.
